questions.q: The dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity $\eta$ is:
questions.solution:
From Newton's law of viscous flow, $F = \eta A \dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

So $\eta = \dfrac{F}{A\,(dv/dx)}$.

Dimensionally: $\dfrac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[L^{2}]\cdot[T^{-1}]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$.

The SI unit is $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and $\mathrm{Pa\,s} = \mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-2}}$, which carries the same dimensions.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs does **not** have the same dimensions?
questions.solution:
Force is $[MLT^{-2}]$. Surface tension is force per unit length, $[MT^{-2}]$ — they differ by a length.

The other three pairs do match:

Impulse $F\,t = [MLT^{-1}]$ and momentum $mv = [MLT^{-1}]$.

Work $[ML^{2}T^{-2}]$ and torque $[ML^{2}T^{-2}]$ — same dimensions, different physical meaning, which is why torque is never written in joules.

Stress and pressure are both force per area, $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$.

questions.q: The length, breadth and thickness of a block are measured as $5.12\ \text{cm}$, $2.1\ \text{cm}$ and $0.035\ \text{cm}$. The volume, to the correct number of significant figures, is:
questions.solution:
The product is $5.12 \times 2.1 \times 0.035 = 0.376320\ \text{cm}^{3}$.

In multiplication, the result carries as many significant figures as the **least** precise factor.

$5.12$ has 3, $2.1$ has 2, $0.035$ has 2 (leading zeros are not significant).

The least is 2, so the answer is $\mathbf{0.38\ \text{cm}^{3}}$.

questions.q: A physical quantity is given by $X = \dfrac{a^{2}b^{3}}{c\sqrt{d}}$. If the percentage errors in $a, b, c, d$ are $1\%, 2\%, 3\%$ and $4\%$, the percentage error in $X$ is:
questions.solution:
For a product of powers, fractional errors **add**, each weighted by the magnitude of its exponent:

$\dfrac{\Delta X}{X} = 2\dfrac{\Delta a}{a} + 3\dfrac{\Delta b}{b} + 1\dfrac{\Delta c}{c} + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta d}{d}$

$= 2(1) + 3(2) + 1(3) + \tfrac{1}{2}(4) = 2 + 6 + 3 + 2 = \mathbf{13\%}$.

Note the exponents are taken as positive whatever their sign — errors never cancel, they accumulate.

questions.q: If force $F$, velocity $v$ and time $T$ are taken as the fundamental units, the dimensional formula of mass is:
questions.solution:
Let $[M] = [F]^{x}[v]^{y}[T]^{z}$.

In ordinary terms $[F] = MLT^{-2}$ and $[v] = LT^{-1}$, so

$M = (MLT^{-2})^{x}(LT^{-1})^{y}(T)^{z}$.

Matching $M$: $x = 1$.

Matching $L$: $x + y = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1$.

Matching $T$: $-2x - y + z = 0 \Rightarrow -2 + 1 + z = 0 \Rightarrow z = 1$.

So mass is $\mathbf{[Fv^{-1}T]}$.

questions.q: A screw gauge has a pitch of $0.5\ \text{mm}$ and $50$ divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is:
questions.solution:
Least count $= \dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{number of circular scale divisions}}$

$= \dfrac{0.5\ \text{mm}}{50} = \mathbf{0.01\ \text{mm}}$.

The pitch is the distance the screw advances in one full turn, so one division of the circular scale advances it by one-fiftieth of that.

questions.q: The quantity $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$ has the dimensions of:
questions.solution:
From Maxwell's equations, the speed of light in vacuum is

$c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$

so the quantity has the dimensions of **velocity**, $[LT^{-1}]$.

Numerically $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi \times 10^{-7})(8.85 \times 10^{-12})}} \approx 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is exactly $c$ — the result that first told Maxwell light was an electromagnetic wave.

questions.q: In an experiment the period of a simple pendulum is measured as $T$ and $g$ is found from $g = 4\pi^{2}L/T^{2}$. If $L$ is measured to $0.5\%$ and $T$ to $1\%$, the error in $g$ is:
questions.solution:
$g \propto \dfrac{L}{T^{2}}$, so

$\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\dfrac{\Delta T}{T} = 0.5 + 2(1) = \mathbf{2.5\%}$.

The period is squared, so its error counts twice — which is why a pendulum experiment times many oscillations rather than one.

questions.q: In the equation $\left(P + \dfrac{a}{V^{2}}\right)(V - b) = RT$, the dimensions of $a$ are:
questions.solution:
Only like quantities may be added, so $\dfrac{a}{V^{2}}$ must have the dimensions of pressure.

$[a] = [P][V^{2}] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}][L^{3}]^{2} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}][L^{6}] = \mathbf{[ML^{5}T^{-2}]}$.

The same rule fixes $b$: it is subtracted from $V$, so $b$ has the dimensions of volume, $[L^{3}]$.

questions.q: The radius of a sphere is measured as $r = 2.1\ \text{cm}$ with an uncertainty of $0.1\ \text{cm}$. What is the percentage error in its volume?
questions.solution:
$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$, so $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\dfrac{\Delta r}{r}$.

$\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} = \dfrac{0.1}{2.1} = 0.0476$

$\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 3 \times 0.0476 = 0.1428 = \mathbf{14.3\%}$ (to 3 significant figures).

The cube is what makes a small length error a large volume error.

questions.q: The density of a material is $8\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Express it in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
questions.solution:
$1\ \mathrm{g} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $1\ \mathrm{cm}^{3} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}^{3}$.

$8\ \dfrac{\mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{cm}^{3}} = 8 \times \dfrac{10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}}{10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}^{3}} = 8 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$

$= \mathbf{8000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}}$.

The factor of $1000$ between $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ is worth memorising — water is $1$ and $1000$ respectively.

questions.q: The frequency $f$ of a stretched string depends on length $L$, tension $F$ and mass per unit length $\mu$ as $f \propto L^{a}F^{b}\mu^{c}$. Find the value of $a$.
questions.solution:
Write the dimensions:

$[T^{-1}] = [L]^{a}[MLT^{-2}]^{b}[ML^{-1}]^{c}$

Matching $M$: $b + c = 0$.

Matching $T$: $-2b = -1 \Rightarrow b = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so $c = -\tfrac{1}{2}$.

Matching $L$: $a + b - c = 0 \Rightarrow a + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow a = \mathbf{-1}$.

This recovers the standard result $f = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{F}{\mu}}$.

questions.q: Four readings of a length are $2.53, 2.55, 2.51$ and $2.57\ \text{cm}$. What is the mean absolute error, in cm?
The time period $T$ of a drop of liquid of density $\rho$ and radius $r$ oscillating under surface tension $S$ is $T = k\,\rho^{x}r^{y}S^{z}$. Find $x + y + z$.
questions.solution:
Dimensions: $[\rho] = ML^{-3}$, $[r] = L$, $[S] = MT^{-2}$.

$[T] = [ML^{-3}]^{x}[L]^{y}[MT^{-2}]^{z}$

Matching $M$: $x + z = 0$.

Matching $T$: $-2z = 1 \Rightarrow z = -\tfrac{1}{2}$, so $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

Matching $L$: $-3x + y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 3x = \tfrac{3}{2}$.

$x + y + z = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{3}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} = \mathbf{\tfrac{3}{2}}$.

The standard result is $T = k\sqrt{\dfrac{\rho r^{3}}{S}}$, which matches these exponents.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the **least count** of an instrument and by a **zero error**. A vernier callipers has $10$ vernier divisions coinciding with $9$ main scale divisions, the main scale being graduated in millimetres. Find its least count. If the instrument reads $0.04\ \text{cm}$ when the jaws are closed, state the kind of zero error and how a reading of $2.36\ \text{cm}$ should be corrected.
questions.solution:
**Least count.** The least count is the smallest change in the measured quantity that an instrument can resolve — the value of one division of its finest scale. Every reading carries an uncertainty of at least this size, so it sets the precision of the measurement.

**Zero error.** A zero error is the reading an instrument gives when the true value is zero — with the jaws of a callipers fully closed, or the screw gauge fully tightened. It is a **systematic** error: it shifts every reading by the same amount, so averaging many readings does not remove it. It is removed by subtracting it.

**Least count of this vernier.**

$10$ vernier divisions $= 9$ main scale divisions $= 9\ \text{mm}$

So $1$ vernier division $= 0.9\ \text{mm}$.

Least count $= 1\ \text{MSD} - 1\ \text{VSD} = 1.0 - 0.9 = 0.1\ \text{mm} = \mathbf{0.01\ \text{cm}}$.

**The zero error.** The instrument reads $+0.04\ \text{cm}$ when it should read zero, so this is a **positive zero error**.

**Correcting the reading.** The correction is the negative of the zero error, so it is subtracted:

True reading $= 2.36 - 0.04 = \mathbf{2.32\ \text{cm}}$.

Had the error been negative, say $-0.04\ \text{cm}$, the same rule would **add** $0.04$ to every reading.
